proposals.proposal:
Open the Daily Blog Post workflow file and read the most recent failure log. The most common causes for this class of CI failure are: a rotated API key that was not updated in GitHub Secrets, a changed branch name, or a Node/Python version mismatch after a dependency bump. The fix is a single-line correction in the workflow YAML or a secret rotation, not a rebuild. Because .github/workflows/* is in the blocked paths list, Joel must apply this fix manually. Fred's role here is to flag the exact failure class so Joel knows where to look.

Check the failed run at 2026-07-07T06:55:24Z. Look at the step that errored. If the error is "API key invalid" or a 401, rotate the MailerLite or OpenAI secret in Settings > Secrets. If the error is a file-not-found on the queue directory, the queue path in the script has drifted from the actual content directory. Either way, the fix touches one line.

proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I track every penny and still feel like it's not enough?"
pubDate: 2026-07-08
description: "You know your numbers. You have a spreadsheet. You check it more than you check your messages. So why does it feel like the ground is always about to shift?"
tags: ["money vigilance", "behavioural finance", "spending anxiety"]
---

You opened your banking app this morning before you got out of bed.

Not because you needed to. You knew roughly what was in there. You checked it anyway.

This is not a discipline problem. The discipline is obvious. The savings rate is real, the budget is colour-coded, the ISA gets topped up in the first week of the month without fail. None of that is in question.

What is in question is why doing all of it correctly still produces a low, persistent hum of financial dread.

Researchers in behavioural economics call this pattern money vigilance. It shows up in people who grew up watching money disappear faster than it arrived, or who learned early that the gap between fine and not-fine was narrower than adults let on. The brain learned to scan for threat. It got good at it. It kept doing it long after the original threat was gone.

The checking is not irrational. It made complete sense once.

What it costs now is the gap between what the numbers actually say and what the body is prepared to believe. You can have six months of expenses in savings and still feel one unexpected bill away from a version of yourself you never want to be again.

That gap is not a character flaw. It is a very logical response to an old set of conditions, running in a context where those conditions no longer apply.

The work is not to stop tracking. The work is to notice what you are actually looking for when you check, and whether the number you find ever fully answers the question.

Joel Burgess, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner, works with people in their late twenties and thirties who are doing the right things financially and still cannot settle into it. If that is where you are, the quiz at the top of this page is a reasonable place to start.
